findings.situation: A married filer filing as head of household lived in Texas during 2025, but the spouse lived all year in a non-community-property state (common, since a HOH spouse must have lived apart for the last six months). The filer truthfully answers yes, and household.hoh_cp_married flags them for refusal.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 23: "If you and your spouse lived in a community property state, you must usually follow state law to determine what is community income and what is separate income."
findings.why: The text's condition is that you and your spouse lived in a community property state. The question asks only whether "you" lived in one, so it brings in married filers whose spouse never lived there.

findings.situation: A filer lived in Arizona from January to March 2025 while single, then moved to Ohio and married there in November. They truthfully answer yes, and household.hoh_cp_married (married at end of 2025 and the answer is yes) flags them.
findings.source_text: Question: "Did you live in a community property state ... at any time in 2025?"; i1040gi p. 23: "If you and your spouse lived in a community property state..."
findings.why: Community income arises only while the spouses were married and living in the community property state. 'At any time in 2025' also counts residence there before the marriage. Unlike cp_not_joint, hoh_cp_married has no 'while married' limit.

findings.situation: A filer whose spouse died in 2025 while both lived in a community property state, and who is not filing jointly, answers No because the marriage ended by death, not by divorce or legal separation.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 23, Community Property States: "If you and your spouse lived in a community property state, you must usually follow state law to determine what is community income and what is separate income."
findings.why: The text's condition covers any part of 2025 spent married and living in a community property state, however the marriage ended. The wording 'before a divorce or legal separation' tells a widowed filer the question is not about them, so the line gets No when it needs Yes.

findings.situation: A registered domestic partner in Nevada, Washington or California truthfully answers No because they were never married, although community income rules apply to them.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 23: "A registered domestic partner in Nevada, Washington, or California must generally report half the combined community income of the individual and their domestic partner. See Form 8958 and Pub. 555."
findings.why: The question asks only about marriage, so a registered domestic partner gives No. The text still requires a Form 8958/Pub. 555 community income split, which is the situation this line exists to refuse.

findings.situation: A filer who lived in a community property state while married to a spouse who lived in a non-community-property state answers Yes.
findings.source_text: Question: "Were you married at any time during 2025 ... while you lived in a community property state"; i1040gi p. 23: "If you and your spouse lived in a community property state"
findings.why: The text's condition requires that both spouses lived in a community property state. The question asks only where the filer lived, so it brings in Yes answers the text's condition does not cover.

findings.situation: A couple obtained a final divorce in 2025 only to file as unmarried, intending to remarry each other in 2026, and did remarry in 2026.
findings.source_text: p501 p. 6, Divorce and remarriage: "you and your spouse must file as married individuals in both years."
findings.why: The question tells the filer to "Answer No if, by December 31, you were divorced under a final decree." findings.situation: A filer whose spouse died in 2025 remarried later in 2025 and was divorced from the new spouse by December 31, 2025, then claims married filing jointly. A truthful Yes satisfies the death-in-2025 path even though remarriage bars a joint return with the deceased spouse.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 13: "Your spouse died in 2025 and you didn't remarry in 2025."; p501 p. 6: "If you remarried before the end of the tax year, you can file a joint return with your new spouse. Your deceased spouse's filing status is married filing separately for that year."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the spouse died in 2025, so its Yes covers more filers than the joint-return condition, which also requires no remarriage in 2025. Filers who remarried and are no longer married at year end get the joint return allowed wrongly.

findings.situation: A filer whose divorce became final earlier in 2025, and whose former spouse then died later in 2025, could read 'your spouse' as including the ex-spouse and answer Yes.
findings.source_text: Question: "Did your spouse die in 2025?"; p501 p. 6: "If you are divorced under a final decree by the last day of the year, you are considered unmarried for the whole year."
findings.why: If the filer counts the former spouse, the Yes is refused and blocks a valid single or head of household return. The wording does not say the person must still have been the filer's spouse when they died.

findings.situation: A filer who chose married filing jointly reads help that says the question is asked only for single or head of household and that a Yes is refused, even though the joint-return path needs a Yes.
findings.source_text: Help: "Asked when your filing status is single or head of household; a Yes is refused"; question: "(Asked when ... filing jointly although not married at the end of 2025.)"; i1040gi p. 13: "Your spouse died in 2025 and you didn't remarry in 2025."
findings.why: The help and the question describe when the question is asked in conflicting ways. A widowed joint filer may answer No to avoid the stated refusal, and that No would disqualify the joint return they are allowed to file.

findings.situation: A couple divorced under a final decree in late 2025 only so they could file as unmarried, and they intend to and do remarry each other in 2026; the filer truthfully answers that they were unmarried at the end of 2025.
findings.source_text: p501 p. 6, Divorce and remarriage: "If you obtain a divorce for the sole purpose of filing tax returns as unmarried individuals, and at the time of divorce you intend to and do, in fact, remarry each other in the next tax year, you and your spouse must file as married individuals in both years."
findings.why: The question asks only whether the filer was unmarried at year end and does not mention this rule. The truthful answer is Yes, but the text treats the filer as married, so household.hoh_eligible must not be true.

findings.situation: A filer in a registered domestic partnership or civil union, which is not denominated as a marriage under state law, is asked whether they were 'unmarried' at the end of 2025.
findings.source_text: p501 p. 6, Definition of marriage: "Individuals who have entered into a registered domestic partnership, civil union, or other similar relationship that isn't denominated as a marriage ... aren't lawfully married for federal tax purposes"
findings.why: The question does not say how such relationships are treated. An ordinary partner could reasonably answer No, seeing the partnership as a marriage, or Yes, seeing themselves as legally unmarried. The text requires Yes.

findings.situation: The filer's spouse was a nonresident alien during 2025, and the couple made the choice to treat the spouse as a resident in a prior year; that choice is still in effect, but no new election was made for 2025.
findings.source_text: i1040gi p. 14: "Also check the box and enter their name if you and your nonresident spouse made the choice to be treated as residents in a prior year and the choice remains in effect"; p501 p. 9: "You are considered married if you choose to treat your spouse as a resident alien."
findings.why: The wording 'you did not elect to treat your spouse as a resident alien' can be read as asking only about an election for 2025. On that reading the filer answers Yes, while a continuing prior-year choice makes them considered married.
